questions.question: How many seconds are there in a leap year (366 days)?
questions.knowledgeNote: Standard conversion used in physics: 1 year = Ï€ Ã— 10â· s (approximate, for order-of-magnitude)
questions.answer: **Seconds in a leap year:** 1 day = 24 × 60 × 60 = 86 400 s. 366 days × 86 400 s = **31 622 400 s** (= 3.16224 × 10⁷ s). **Deep point:** the ordinary year (365 d) gives 31 536 000 s — the leap day adds exactly one more 86 400; both are worth memorising to one significant figure (~3.16 × 10⁷ s).

questions.question: The SI dimensional unit kg m2 s-2 represents: (a) work (b) force (c) power (d) impulse
questions.solution:
**Correct option: (a) work.**

**Step 1 — Check each quantity:**
- Force: $F = ma = \text{kg m s}^{-2}$ — does **not** match.
- Work: $W = Fs = \text{kg m s}^{-2} \times \text{m} = \text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-2}$ — **matches**. ✓
- Power: $P = W/t = \text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-3}$ — does not match.
- Impulse: $Ft = \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ — does not match.

**Step 2 — Conclusion:** $\text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-2} = \text{N m} = \text{J}$, so it is **work (and energy)**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Kilogram metre squared per second squared equals newton metre, which is the joule used for work and energy.
questions.answer: **kg m² s⁻²** = (kg·m/s²)·m = N·m = **joule** ⟹ **(a) work**. **Check the others:** force is kg·m·s⁻² (no m²); power is kg·m²·s⁻³ (one s more); impulse is kg·m·s⁻¹ (one m fewer). **Deep point:** reading a dimensional formula as a product of named units — here N × m — is faster than matching letters; kg m² s⁻² is also the dimension of energy in *every* form (kinetic, potential, heat).
